articles.title: Former WSU student sentenced to three months in jail for voyeurism felony
articles.description: A former WSU student who secretly recorded men in a campus dormitory bathroom has been sentenced to three months in jail, the maximum jail term allowed in the case. Juan Velasco, 20, pleaded guilty Aug. 21 to one count of first-degree felony voyeurism in Whitman County Superior Court. Judge Roger Sandberg sentenced Velasco on Oct. 2 to three months in jail and one year of probation following his release. Sandberg also ordered Velasco to register as a sex offender for 10 years, undergo a psychosexual evaluation and comply with recommended treatment. The case began in April 2025, when a student discovered Velasco recording him in the third-floor showers of Stephenson South, per the records from the case. The victim recorded Velasco in return and confronted him. Two additional photos the victim took helped investigators identify Velasco. Court documents also say that during the investigation, Velasco acknowledged recording the victim and other men without their permission. Investigators also found footage of Velasco apparently practicing camera angles between bathroom stalls, searches related to secretly recording in dormitory bathrooms and two additional videos depicting men inside bathroom stalls. Velasco initially faced three counts of first-degree voyeurism. Prosecutors dropped two counts as part of a plea agreement, in part because investigators could not identify the other victims. The identified victim agreed with the prosecution's sentencing recommendation, according to statements made in court. WSU police investigated the case. Velasco was suspended from the university following the misconduct and had been living in Toppenish, Washington.

articles.title: Teacher allegedly filmed hundreds of kids using toilets
articles.description: A primary school teacher has been accused of secretly filming young children as they used the school bathroom more than 357 times on hidden spy cameras. Timothy Blamires, 33, appeared before Melbourne Magistrates' Court on Friday 9 October, for a brief hearing before his matter was adjourned to November 20. Charge sheets released by the court revealed the extent of the teacher's alleged crimes committed over six months at Kingswood Primary School, at Dingley Village. Blamires is accused of installing the spy cameras inside fragrance dispensers in school toilets and filming children between October 13, 2025 and April 21. Court documents allege he recorded "in excess" of 34 prepubescent children on October 13, 2025, more than 188 children a week later on October 20, and over 60 children two days after that on October 22. On March 30, he is accused of recording in excess of 74 children using the spy cams. A cleaner replacing an odour dispenser's fragrance inside the male toilets on April 28 allegedly discovered the hidden camera inside, which had a wire connected to a hard drive. She placed it into a plastic bag and put it on the principal's desk before police were called. While officers were on their way, Blamires is accused of taking the camera and putting it inside a drawer in a sick bay before returning to his class to teach. The odour dispenser was allegedly found inside his backpack at the school after his arrest, and police seized devices from his home including laptops, phones and tablets. Blamires has been charged with 16 offences, including six counts of installing a spy cam, five counts of producing child abuse material, four counts of possessing child abuse material and one count of refusing to comply with a police direction to hand over access codes to devices. He was denied bail in May after a magistrate found his risks could not be reduced to an acceptable level, pointing to difficulties in enforcing a ban on internet access. 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) National Sexual Abuse and Redress Support Service 1800 211 028

pendingReview.title: The weird Reno invention that suddenly makes perfect sense
pendingReview.description: Here's what to bring on a road trip in case you have to use a dirty restroom. I'm not necessarily out here looking for weird ideas to write about. These things just fall into my lap. For example: Did you know that Reno is suddenly a hotbed of public restroom innovation? It's true. First, there's the Peep No More, the green/red indicator that shows whether restroom stalls are occupied or not. That was a game-changer in 2011. We no longer had to walk hunched over down the line of stalls, looking for shoes and desperately avoiding eye contact with stall occupants. ("No, I'm not skulking around the restroom peeping into stalls, like some kind of creep! I was actually just ... uh, about to bend over and tie my shoe, right here in the restroom, a totally normal place to do this.") And after that, who can forget about the ... uh ... OK, maybe we're only at two restroom breakthroughs for Reno so far. But still, that's a lot for one mid-sized city! What has Spokane done to improve the restroom experience? Nothing, probably. (I will not research this.) As for the next big thing ... it's weird that nobody has invented it already. Sometimes when we touch, the honesty's too much Every time I'm in a public restroom with manual flushing, faucet knobs and do-it-yourself paper-towel-dispensing, I think, "Am I in some kind of time-capsule restroom from 1985? Where's the tech?" Theoretically, restroom visits should all be 100% hands-free experience. That is, except for that one other thing we touch. The grossest thing. The toilet seat. With that, it's just chaos. It's like some sort of post-apocalyptic nightmare. Just lawless. And nobody was doing anything about it. That is, until Leon Abravanel and Sean Fannan got together to develop the Seat Lift, a foot pedal that automatically raises and lowers the seat on public toilets. "It's a subconscious problem because we just deal with it," Abravanel said. He'd had the idea for the apparatus as part of an entrepreneurship course while earning his MBA. Years later, both he and Fannan were in search of their next big idea. Fannan wasn't on board at first. "Originally he said, yeah, I don't know," Abravanel recalled. "And then I took him to a gas station bathroom -- two friends walking into the bathroom, it looked suspicious, right? -- but I had to give him the visual of what we're solving." Pedals everywhere The idea is simple. The Seat Lift is a foot pedal for men's and unisex restrooms that lifts the seat if you're standing up to pee, then lowers it when you walk away. OK, it's actually fairly complicated. They tested nearly a dozen materials before settling on durable industrial-grade magnesium coated with an antimicrobial finish, able to handle restroom cleaning chemicals, and designed to be compatible with basically every toilet in the United States and Canada. Why test almost an entire continent's worth of toilets? Because that's the vision for Abravanel and Fannan: near-universal foot pedals, replacing the universal "flipping the toilet seat up with your shoe, but gentle enough that it stays up and doesn't crash back down, flinging pee everywhere" method. Long story short: These guys think that the devices might be everywhere in no time. "It's like Koala Care," Abravanel said, referring to the baby-changing station brand. "It's the same thing. It shows that you care about parents being able to change their kids in a hygienic way. "That's kind of our goal as a business ... where people, obviously years from now, expect this to be part of the restroom experience." Once he mentioned the baby-changing stations, it clicked. I got it. (Sometimes I don't immediately get the utility of things. Three decades ago, I remember thinking that sending photos via text was too niche of an idea to catch on.) But universal baby-changing stations -- of course. We didn't have those, and definitely not in men's restrooms. They started showing up when I became a dad, but not nearly enough. I changed several diapers on sink countertops when there were no other options, getting me a bunch of angry stares. ("Please, by all means, complain to the management about this! I have no other options, and I am deliberately making this everyone's problem now.") In other words, I'm a believer. I think these really might be everywhere. Reno 911? Or Reno No. 1 and 2? Maybe this is Reno's next identity, becoming the Silicon Valley of restrooms. Personally, I'm fine with it. Better yet, we could make it our thing to solve one weird public restroom issue every decade or so -- enough to keep things innovative, but not enough that we become known as Toilet Town USA. For Abravanel, Northern Nevada was as good a place as any to launch a product aimed at a universal problem. "Northern Nevada is a great place to start," he said. "We love being a Northern Nevada company and the problem is the same everywhere in the world. So why not start here?" He pointed to Reno's growth and evolution over the last decade. "It's really impressive to see how this town has transitioned from what it was to what it's becoming," he said. "It's ripe for opportunity." Your move, Spokane. Email your worst public restroom experiences to bmcginness@rgj.com. Brett McGinness is the engagement editor for the Reno Gazette Journal. He's also the writer of The Reno Memo -- a free newsletter about news in the Biggest Little City.

pendingReview.title: Gymnastics coach sentenced to 90 years for secretly recording girls
pendingReview.description: The case has revived questions about whether USA Gymnastics and SafeSport adequately responded to warnings about Gardner. PURVIS, Mississippi - A former youth gymnastics coach was sentenced to 90 years in federal prison Wednesday for secretly recording young female gymnasts undressing and using the bathroom at a Mississippi gym. Gymnastics coach sentenced to prison for secretly recording girls Big picture view: U.S. District Judge Kristi Johnson handed down the maximum possible sentence to Sean Gardner, 39, ordering him to serve 30 years for each of three federal child pornography production charges to which he pleaded guilty. The sentence is likely to keep Gardner behind bars for the rest of his life. Sean Gardner admits to placing hidden camera in bathroom The backstory: Gardner admitted to placing a hidden camera in a bathroom at a gymnastics studio in Purvis, Mississippi, between December 2017 and April 2018. Investigators said he recorded videos showing close-up images of at least 10 minors who were naked or undressing. Authorities recovered the videos from his computers years later while investigating allegations of sexual abuse involving gymnasts in Iowa. Before his arrest, Gardner was a prominent figure in youth gymnastics. He coached at Chow's Gymnastics and Dance Institute in West Des Moines, Iowa, founded by renowned coach Liang "Chow" Qiao, who has helped develop Olympic champions. Gardner worked with several promising young gymnasts and directed an annual winter competition in Iowa that attracted hundreds of athletes. SafeSport temporarily suspended Gardner in 2022 after a gymnast at Chow's alleged sexual abuse. Chow's fired him that year. Gardner was arrested last summer by the FBI. Case brings back renewed scrutiny around athlete safety Why you should care: His arrest has renewed scrutiny of USA Gymnastics and other organizations responsible for protecting young athletes from abuse by coaches in positions of authority. An Associated Press investigation found that concerns about Gardner dated back to 2017, yet the U.S. Center for SafeSport did not sanction him until 2022. The investigation also raised questions about why a proposed lifetime coaching ban was not finalized before his arrest in 2025. The parallels to the Larry Nassar scandal center on institutional accountability. The Nassar scandal exposed serious failures by organizations and officials who received warnings about the former USA Gymnastics team doctor's abuse. Nassar sexually abused more than 100 victims under the guise of medical treatment, and a 2021 Justice Department inspector general report criticized the FBI's handling of allegations against him. Nassar is serving decades in prison for convictions in state and federal courts.
